definition: An infection that inflames the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus.
general_symptoms: High fever (up to 105 degrees Fahrenheit or 40 degrees Celsius)
Cough with yellow, green or bloody mucus
Rapid breathing or shortness of breath
Chest pain and/or abdominal pain, especially with coughing or deep breathing
general_diagnosis_methods: Health history and physical examination (listening to lungs with a stethoscope)
general_treatments: Draining fluids (done with a catheter or surgery)
Pain relievers and fever reducers (like ibuprofen and acetaminophen)
general_outlook: Viral pneumonia often gets better on its own
Most symptoms of bacterial pneumonia usually start to get better within a day or two after starting treatment
Some symptoms, like cough and fatigue, may linger for several weeks
It may take six to eight weeks to feel back to normal if you’ve been hospitalized

May have lingering health issues after recovery, such as trouble with physical activity (shortness of breath or reduced stamina), worsening of cardiovascular disease, or general decline in quality of life
Children who’ve recovered from pneumonia have an increased risk of chronic lung diseases
Can be life-threatening if left untreated
complications: Bacteria in your bloodstream, which can lead to sepsis and organ failure
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and respiratory failure
prevention: Getting vaccinated (Pneumococcal vaccines, COVID-19, flu, childhood vaccinations)
Quitting smoking and avoiding secondhand smoke
Washing hands with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand sanitizer
Avoiding close contact and sharing items with other people if either of you has a contagious disease
Asking healthcare providers about reducing infection risk during hospital stays
Getting treated for other infections or health conditions
living_with: Follow up with your healthcare provider if you have ongoing health concerns after recovering

causes: Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections (MRSA, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Serratia marcescens, Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
Fungal infections (Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Coccidioides / Valley fever)
Aspiration of solid food, liquids, spit or vomit
Air sacs filling with oily substances

demographic_manifestations.definition: Pneumonia presenting in pediatric populations, often showing distinct clinical signs and requiring age-specific monitoring.
causes: Group B strep bacteria (usually in newborns)
Cold and flu viruses (rhinoviruses, human metapneumovirus, adenoviruses, influenza and parainfluenza viruses)
specific_symptoms: Increased work of breathing (retractions / skin between ribs pulling inward with each breath)
Not wanting to feed or drink
Low muscle tone (making them feel more 'floppy')
Cyanosis (bluish/pale light skin, gray/whitish dark skin)
diagnosis: Physical exam (listening to breathing with a stethoscope)
Lab tests for viruses and bacteria, electrolytes, and blood gas levels
treatments: Medications for other symptoms (fever, pain, inflammation)
complications: Needing to stay in a hospital
Needing breathing support like mechanical ventilation
Follow-up infections while immune system is weak
Higher risk of having pneumonia or other respiratory diseases in the future
outlook: Outlook is generally good, especially with timely diagnosis and treatment
About 1 in 5 children with pneumonia need to stay in the hospital
Most children who need to stay in the hospital are under 2 years old
Recovery time for children with pneumonia varies widely
prevention: Limiting exposure to others who are ill
